sly

/sly/ — rhymes with why · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sly describes someone who is clever in a sneaky, crafty way, often to trick or outwit others.

With a sly wink, the magician slipped the card into my pocket.

Example

With a sly grin, she switched the salt shaker with the sugar, knowing her brother would not notice until he stirred his coffee.

Sly perfectly captures clever, cunning trickery designed to outwit someone. It's not just deception—it's the clever, often playful scheme to fool someone in a witty way.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tricky: Tricky warns you that a person or problem is likely to use tricks or hidden catches to fool you. Sly points at the manner instead: quietly clever in a sneaky way, with a playful edge, so a sly move charms even as it outwits.

wily: Wily describes someone full of clever tricks learned over long experience — the wily veteran who has seen every ploy. Sly needs no long career: it is the quick, knowing sneakiness of a single trick or glance, lighter and more playful than a strategist's craft.

mischievous: Mischievous means fond of playful trouble — pranks and teasing done mostly for fun, often in plain sight. Sly keeps the fun but adds concealment: a sly trickster is quietly outwitting someone and hides how much they know.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

straightforward: open and direct, hiding nothing at all

candid: honestly speaking your true thoughts openly

Where it sits · how much hidden trickery is involved — clever → cunning → crafty → sly

clever vs. sly: Clever is much weaker than sly; clever is simply being quick-minded, while sly turns that quickness toward tricking and outwitting others.

cunning vs. sly: Cunning is nearly as strong as sly, but cunning names a talent for planning schemes, while sly adds an extra layer of secrecy — a sly person hides even the fact that they are scheming at all.

crafty vs. sly: Crafty is slightly weaker than sly: a crafty plan is skillfully designed to outwit someone, while a sly one is also carried out with hidden, knowing mischief.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sly (slœgr)

Root — sly (slœgr): cunning, crafty; literally 'able to strike' (Old Norse)

Put it together

Put it together: Sly comes whole from Old Norse slœgr, 'cunning, crafty' — literally 'able to strike.' Someone sly has that same crafty precision: clever enough to land a trick before anyone sees it coming.

Use the root in a new word: sleight

Use the root in a new word: sleight: The magician's sleight of hand fooled the whole audience — sleight and sly both descend from the same Old Norse word for cunning skill.

Word Choice

neutral / informal

Use sly for clever trickery meant to outwit someone, often with a playful or mischievous tone. It's less harsh than 'cunning' and less serious than 'crafty.' For straightforward deception without cleverness, use 'deceptive' or 'dishonest.'
